Aviation Stack Exchange answer a/14559 (2D slope 2pi; slope increases slightly with thickness)

summary: The 2*pi/beta core is textbook thin-airfoil theory with the Prandtl-Glauert compressibility correction. The thickness factor (1 + 0.77*t/c) has the right sign of the inviscid thickness effect but the 0.77 constant could not be traced to any published source, and the code ignores the viscous slope reduction, so it overpredicts real section slopes by ~15-20% at F1 conditions.

citations.title: Parasitic drag / Zero-lift drag coefficient

summary: No published equation of this form was found; it is a project fit. The baseline 0.006 matches the typical minimum profile drag of smooth airfoil sections at Re of several million (NACA R-824 data), and the trends (drag grows with camber and thickness) are physically correct, but the specific linear/quadratic penalties are heuristic and misrepresent drag-bucket behaviour.

name: Reynolds-number drag correction

citations.title: Skin friction drag (Prandtl one-seventh-power law cf = 0.0576*Re_x^(-1/5))
Boundary-Layer Theory
citations.url_or_reference: Pergamon/McGraw-Hill; record verified via Open Library; cited for Prandtl-Schlichting cf = 0.455/(log10 Re)^2.58

summary: Power-law decay of friction drag with Reynolds number is textbook boundary-layer theory (turbulent flat plate: cf ~ Re^(-1/5)), so the form is grounded, but the -0.15 exponent is tuned and is applied to total profile drag rather than the friction component. The two branches are discontinuous at Re = 1e6 (factor jumps 1.2 -> 1.0, a ~17% step), right in the F1 front-wing Reynolds range.

citations.title: Aerodynamics of a Double-Element Wing in Ground Effect, AIAA Journal 41(6):1007-1016

summary: The existence of an optimal slot gap and the boundary-layer re-energising role of slot flow are established (Smith 1975), but the Gaussian efficiency curve, the 2%-chord optimum, and especially cl_multiplier = circulation_boost*sqrt(velocity_ratio) have no published counterpart; the sqrt of a velocity ratio multiplying a lift coefficient is dimensionally arbitrary. The multiplier varies only from ~1.54 to ~1.95, so the model barely responds to gap variation despite calling it 'physics-based'.

name: Cantilever beam first natural frequency

citations.title: Formulas for Natural Frequency and Mode Shape (Table 8-1, cantilever)
citations.url_or_reference: Van Nostrand Reinhold; record verified via Open Library; beta1*L = 1.8751 also verified numerically in this review

citations.title: Euler-Bernoulli beam theory (free vibration; beta_n := (mu*omega^2/EI)^(1/4); cantilever example)

summary: The formula is exactly the Euler-Bernoulli cantilever first-mode result (beta1*L = 1.8751, verified numerically). However the code passes the full span as L: a centreline-mounted wing is two cantilevers of span/2 (f scales as 1/L^2, so the estimate is 4x too low; a clamped-clamped model would be ~6.4x higher). The statics use simply-supported WL/8 while the dynamics use cantilever BCs, and laminate/tip-mass effects are ignored.

citations.title: Buckling (plate-buckling derivation: sigma_cr = k_cr*pi^2*E/(12*(1-nu^2)*(b/t)^2), k_cr=(mb/a+a/mb)^2, min k=4)
Theory of Elastic Stability, 2nd ed., Ch. 7 (buckling of thin plates)

citations.url_or_reference: McGraw-Hill; record verified via Open Library

citations.title: Mechanics of Composite Materials (orthotropic laminate analysis)
citations.url_or_reference: Taylor & Francis; record verified via Open Library

summary: This is the classical plate-buckling stress with the buckling coefficient implicitly set to k=1, which matches only the wide-column limit (both long edges free). Supported skin panels have k=4, a free-edged cover has k~0.425, so k=1 is 4x off each bounding case. The panel width b is set to the full root chord (no intermediate support), and an isotropic E with nu=0.3 is used for a CFRP laminate where orthotropic D-matrix buckling analysis is standard.

citations.title: Tsai-Wu failure criterion (standard anisotropic composite criterion)

summary: SF = allowable/applied stress is the standard definition, and sqrt(sigma^2 + 3*tau^2) is exactly the von Mises equivalent for combined bending+shear - correct usage for isotropic ductile metals. But the wing is explicitly CFRP: von Mises is not a valid failure theory for anisotropic composites (Tsai-Wu/Hashin/max-stress with directional allowables is standard), and the fatigue check omits mean-stress (Goodman) and spectrum effects, so it is a screening check only.
